All, therefore, who applaud themselves in strength of body and worldly power, and say with the devil, By strength I will do it, will be plundered on the day of the wrath of the Lord and brought to nothing. Ashkelon also, which is called weighed, or murderous fire, when the day of the wrath of the Lord comes, will feel the measure of its crime and will be pressed down by the same weight with which it acted. And because it burned to shed blood, and caused many souls to stumble, and in it was fulfilled: The man of blood and deceit the Lord will abhor, it will not be plundered like Gaza, but, reduced to desolation, it will be burned to dust by the fires of Gehenna. Ashdod too, which in Hebrew is called esdod and in our language means fire of generation, will be laid waste in clear light; for it burned with lust and raged in the fire of generation. And because all adulterers, their hearts are like an oven, and they have been wounded by burning arrows, not in darkness, not in a hidden judgment, but at noon, that is, when the saints will receive their full brightness, they will be cast forth into darkness, and they will not have the fellowship of the saints. But Ekron, which is interpreted barrenness, or uprooting, because it bore no fruits and by the perversity of its teaching uprooted very many, will itself also be uprooted. Understand all these varieties in the vices and sins of souls, and that on the day of judgment the fire will test of what sort each one's work is.
Commentary on Zephaniah

Woe to you who inhabit the cord of the sea, nation of the lost; the word of the Lord is upon you, Canaan, land of the Philistines, and I will destroy you so that there is no inhabitant. And the cord of the sea will be a resting place of shepherds, and folds of flocks; and the cord will be his who has remained of the house of Judah; there they will feed, in the houses of Ashkelon they will rest at evening, for the Lord their God will visit them and will turn back their captivity. LXX: Woe to you who inhabit the cord of the sea, sojourners of the Cretans; the word of the Lord is upon you, Canaan, land of the foreigners, and I will destroy you from habitation. And Crete will be a pasture of shepherds, and a fold of flocks, and the cord of the sea will be for those who are left of the house of Judah; upon them they will feed in the houses of Ashkelon; after noon they will turn aside from the face of the sons of Judah, for the Lord their God will visit them and will turn back their captivity. As regards the history, it is not difficult to interpret, because above he had said: Gaza will be destroyed, and Ashkelon into a wilderness. Ashdod they will cast out at noon, and Ekron will be uprooted. Four great cities of Philistia having been named, it is plain that the word of the Lord is now addressed to the province itself in general, and that it is foretold to it: Woe to you who inhabit the cord of the sea, when the Babylonian comes, for those too who dwell beside the sea will perish and be carried off. And that the land of the Philistines is the land of Canaan, no one doubts. And I will destroy you, he says, so that there is no inhabitant; and you who rejoiced at the overthrow of Judea will come to such devastation that all your most fortified cities will become folds of shepherds. And after the Lord has visited his people and made them return under Zerubbabel and Joshua, and they have built the temple and raised up Jerusalem again, you will be so uncultivated, and so covered with briars and nettles, that shepherds from the remnant of the Jews will rest in Ashkelon after noon and make their flocks lie down in a once noble city; and this will happen because the Lord will visit his people and turn back its captivity. Whether this happened or not, that is for God to see. For it is not now our purpose to weave together the truth of the history, but to make known to our own people what we have received from the Hebrews.
Commentary on Zephaniah

Again, where we said: And the cord of the sea will be a resting place of shepherds, and all the translators agreed with this translation, in the LXX is written: And Crete will be a pasture of the flock, and a fold of flocks. Therefore, comparing spiritual things with spiritual, and keeping to the path of the common edition that we once began, we ask whether we have read the name of Crete elsewhere in the holy Scriptures. And, unless I am mistaken, this is ready to hand: Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies. This testimony is true. Those who waver and are carried about by every wind of doctrine, in the deceit of men, in the craftiness of error, though they ought to have dwelt in the land of confession, that is, in the land of Judea, chose rather to be strangers of the Cretans, who are beaten this way and that by the various waves of the sea, and sound with Corybantian bronze, and are, according to the Apostle: Like a tinkling cymbal. And because they are strangers of the Cretans, therefore the word of God, that is, a threat, comes to them, and they are called the land of Canaan, always in the surge, always in motion, and the land of the foreigners; for, being alien from God, they dwell in the cord of the sea and in the region of Crete. And so the word of God comes to them, either at the consummation and end of the world, or daily through churchmen and those who can say with the Apostle: Or do you seek a proof of Christ, who speaks in me? so that they may be cast out of Crete and be destroyed from their former habitations, and that region which formerly held a lost flock may begin to be a fold of the flocks of Christ; and Judah, that is, true confession, may dwell in the cords of the sea. And when the world has now begun to be at evening, and of many called few are chosen, and those who are now called the remnant of the house of Judah have fed those who formerly fed in the sea and in Crete and in falsehood, they will turn aside into the houses of Ashkelon, that is, where formerly the fire of the devil and the blood of the slain flowed. For Ashkelon is interpreted murderous fire. And this will happen because the Lord will visit his people, and those who before were easily caught by the sophisms of heretics will, as if coming out of captivity, conquer their adversaries and dwell in their tents.
Commentary on Zephaniah

But according to the spiritual sense and the translation of the LXX the understanding is difficult, especially since they also disagree in the interpretation. For where we translated nation of the lost, they said strangers of the Cretans; and where in Hebrew is written goi chorethim, for goi, that is, nation, they read car, that is, stranger; and chorethim, which means of the lost, they took for the name of the island of Crete. Indeed both Aquila and the Fifth Edition translated ἔθνος ὀλέθριον (a destructive nation); and Theodotion ἔθνος ὀλεθρίας (a nation of destruction); Symmachus too ἔθνος ὀλεθρευόμενον (a nation being destroyed), all of which agree with our translation.
Commentary on Zephaniah

But what is read in the LXX, From the face of the sons of Judah, we have marked with an obelus, for it is neither in the Hebrew nor found in any of the translators, and it disturbs the context and the sense of the chapter; not that it would have been difficult to weave a meaning somehow even with this set down; but we have once for all resolved to follow the truth of the translation, and the judgment of the more learned reader rather than that of the crowd.
Commentary on Zephaniah

I have heard the reproach of Moab and the blasphemies of the sons of Ammon, with which they reproached my people, and they were magnified over their borders. Therefore, as I live, says the Lord God of hosts, the God of Israel, Moab will be as Sodom, and the sons of Ammon as Gomorrah, a dryness of thorns and heaps of salt, and a wilderness for ever; the remnants of my people will plunder them; the residue of my nation will possess them. This will befall them for their pride, because they blasphemed and were magnified over the people of the Lord of hosts. Terrible is the Lord over them, and he will waste away all the gods of the earth, and men will worship him from their place, all the islands of the nations. LXX: I have heard the reproach of Moab and the insults of the sons of Ammon, in which they reproached my people and were magnified over my borders. Therefore, as I live, says the Lord of powers, the God of Israel, Moab will be like Sodom, and the sons of Ammon as Gomorrah, and Damascus left like a heap of the threshing floor, and scattered for ever; and those who are left of my people will plunder them, and the residue of my nation will possess them; this will be to them for their insult, because they reproached and were magnified over the Lord Almighty; the Lord will be manifest over them, and he will destroy all the gods of the nations of the earth, and they will worship him, each from his place, all the islands of the nations. Except for the prophet Daniel, who quite often sees visions of the four kingdoms and sets out their differences under one image after another, Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel do this: after the vision of Judah they turn their prophecy against the other nations that are round about it, and announce, according to the ἰδιώματα (particular characters) of each, what is going to come upon them, and dwell at some length on describing them; and this the prophet Zephaniah now does, briefly indeed, yet in the same order. For after the Philistines, against whom the threat ran on before above, Gaza, he says, will be destroyed, and Ashkelon into a wilderness, Ashdod they will cast out at noon, and Ekron will be uprooted. Now the prophecy is woven against Moab and the sons of Ammon, or, as is added in the LXX, against Damascus, which in Isaiah is called Aram, because by furnishing aid to Nebuchadnezzar they laid waste Judah, trampled its sanctuary, overthrew the temple as well, and, when the people of Israel had been subjugated, blasphemed the Lord. For Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans, after demolishing the cities of the Jews, oppressed the other nations too, and so it came about that those who had insulted the people of God were themselves also pressed by the same straits of evils, and had Judah as a fellow servant, whom they had thought they had as a subject. Therefore, before the captivity comes, while Josiah is still king and Jerusalem and the temple are not yet overthrown, the prophecy is directed against those who insult, so that the evils once suffered by the people of God might be lightened by the evil of the other nations. I have heard, he says, the reproach of Moab, which is now called Areopolis, and the blasphemies of the sons of Ammon, which is itself also a city of Arabia, second after Bozrah, and is called Philadelphia; in which they reproached my people and, having cast out the Jews, extended their own boundaries in their land.
Commentary on Zephaniah

But the man who is learned, and compares spiritual things with spiritual, and seeks not the things that are below but those that are above, and rises with Christ from the underworld, and, putting off the old man, is clothed with the new, will refer the reproaches of Moab and the blasphemies of the sons of Ammon to the masters of doctrines contrary to the Church, who themselves also seem to be of the stock of Abraham, and to have escaped the burning of Sodom and Gomorrah, and to dwell in little Zoar. But because their generation is in darkness, and they cannot look upon the light of truth — for they have turned aside from God the Father, which is interpreted from the names Lot and Moab —, and they have ceased to be sons of God, which is what my people means, and, conceived of incestuous unions in a dark cave, they came into being, therefore to this day, insulting the simplicity of the sons of Judah, they desire to magnify their own possession over its borders; of whom it is said in Proverbs: Do not remove the everlasting boundaries which your fathers set. See the heretics applauding themselves in dialectic and rhetoric and the doctrines of every sophism, despising the rusticity of the Church, and looking down on it as unworthy of their mysteries, which they have fashioned for themselves like idols, and holding it for nothing, and you will not ask what the reproaches of Moab are, and the insults of the sons of Ammon, in which they reproached the people of God.
Commentary on Zephaniah

Now let us return to the LXX translators, and let us compel the Jews, who follow only the history, to explain to us when Moab and the sons of Ammon became like Sodom and Gomorrah, and like heaps of salt, and deserted for ever; they must show the sulphurous rains, the vineyards, the land turned into ashes and embers, and that the sea which is now called Dead flooded over from what were once wells of salt, when the Jews plundered them, when the remaining Israelite peoples possessed them. Or what indignation of the Lord is it, for blasphemy and insults, to waste away and destroy them? Not Moab and Ammon, but the whole earth, so that they may worship him, each from his place, all the islands of the nations? This he will rather bestow on the blasphemers as a benefit, that they may return from error to salvation. But if they wish to say that after the return from Babylon these nations were subjected to the people of Israel, first we shall demand the authority of the Scriptures by which they may prove that this happened; then, when they are quite unable to demonstrate it, we shall grant it to them out of superfluity and say: Suppose that what you say happened; what justice of God would it be that the grandfathers blasphemed and the forefathers reproached, and afterwards it was repaid to the grandsons? Especially since that sentence by which it was formerly said in the law that the sins of the fathers are repaid upon the sons in the third and the fourth generation has been loosed through Ezekiel: As I live, says the Lord; this parable shall no longer be spoken, but the soul that sins, it shall die. And at the same time notice that what was said is a parable, and does not mean what they bring forward on the surface of the letter. But if it is unjust to repay grandsons for what their grandfathers did wrong, how much more unjust is it, according to the folly of the Jews, to hope that this very thing will happen at the consummation of the world, when not their Christ, as they think, but the Antichrist is going to come. For wherever they are hard pressed in the history to show that what was said has been fulfilled, they at once leap over to the future times of Christ, and everything that they cannot explain they promise themselves after many ages; and they say that Moab and the sons of Ammon, and Egypt and the Philistines, and Idumea, which now insult the Jews, are to be punished at that time. Let us ask them, therefore, why God punishes these nations above all, and not the whole world, in which the Jews are scattered far and wide. For if Moab deserves to be chastised for insulting the Jews, and the sons of Ammon and the other nations round about, why is Gaul not chastised? Why does he not put the Britains in the threat? Why are the Spains exempt from punishment? For what reason is nothing said of Italy? Why is there silence about Africa? And to say it once for all, since the whole world holds the Jews captive, what so great a crime have the nations alone committed that are round about it, that they alone above all should be named? These things against the Jews, and as a general explanation in all the prophets wherever any prophecy is spoken against the nations.
Commentary on Zephaniah

And so Moab and Ammon and Damascus, which have prepared themselves against the knowledge of the Lord, and have blasphemed the people of God, and spoken very many insults against it, and wished to extend their borders in the land of the Church and to possess the people of God, will be deserted and destroyed; and the remnant of the people of God, that is, churchmen learned in the Lord's Scriptures, will plunder them, and the residue of the Lord's nation will possess them, and this will be to them for the insult with which they reproached and were magnified against the Lord Almighty. See the clemency, see the mercy of the Lord: he suffers insult, he is blasphemed, his borders are plundered, and what does he do? He sends to the remnant of his people, of whom we have spoken, that he may divide out for himself those who blaspheme him and lead them into his own possession. For it is much better for a fool to serve a wise man, and for his folly to be corrected by the wisdom of the Lord, than for him to be left to his own stupidity.
Commentary on Zephaniah

Therefore, because they have blasphemed me and reproached my people, I, the Lord of hosts, who am able to fulfil what I threaten, and the God of Israel, who myself suffer injury in my people, will make Moab to be as Sodom, and the sons of Ammon as Gomorrah. Let us read visions of this kind in Isaiah and Jeremiah, and we shall find the same things that we now read here. A dryness of thorns and heaps of salt, and a wilderness for ever: in its place the LXX, meaning I know not what, translated: Damascus torn up and left, deceived, unless I am mistaken, by the ambiguity of the word; for dryness, which in Hebrew is called mamasac, if its first letter mem is changed and daleth is taken, has the same remaining letters as Damascus too, and in place of the former word damasec can be read. But it is asked how these cities, that is, Moab and the sons of Ammon, have been reduced to Sodom and Gomorrah, and, like an aridity of thorns and heaps of salt, are not to be built up for ever? And that they were indeed laid waste like Sodom and Gomorrah, there is no difficulty in explaining. But what follows, They will be deserted for ever, either we shall interpret of the destruction of their kingdom — because afterwards, overthrown by the Chaldeans, they lost their kingdom, and then, held either by the Antiochi or by the Ptolemies, they at last bowed their necks to the Roman empire —, or else it must certainly be taken as said ὑπερβολικῶς (hyperbolically); for lolam signifies both eternity and an age, so that it can be taken both for one age and for some length of time, and for one lifetime. And those who are left of the people of Israel will lay them waste, and will possess the once blaspheming auxiliaries of the Chaldeans.
Commentary on Zephaniah

Now what we said above, that Damascus is not found in the Hebrew, nor in any other translator, we shall prove also from the very order of Scripture. For to what he had said, I have heard the reproach of Moab, and the blasphemies of the sons of Ammon, he afterwards related: That Moab will be as Sodom, and the sons of Ammon as Gomorrah. As for what follows, then, And Damascus deserted, like a heap of the threshing floor, he ought also to have said something about Damascus beforehand, so that, just as he had said of the two nations, Moab will be as Sodom, and the sons of Ammon as Gomorrah, whose sins he had already stated before. So he would also have described either the reproaches or the blasphemies of Damascus, so that afterwards he might be seen to inflict punishment deservedly. But this very phrase too, Like a heap of the threshing floor, which in Greek is said ὡς θιμωνιὰ ἄλωνος, we think the LXX translated ἀλος, that is, of salt; but that by unskilled men, who took θιμωνίαν, that is, a heap of grain or of crops, in place of ἀλος, with the two letters ω and ν added, as though to follow on from the crops, ἄλωνος, that is, of the threshing floor, was set down. Let this be said about the variety and error of interpretation, and about the difficulty of the history.
Commentary on Zephaniah

And so the Lord swore by himself, saying: As I live, says the Lord. And beautifully, to distinguish himself from the dead gods, who are called idols, the God of Israel, that is, of the people that sees God, says that he lives; whereas these blaspheming nations, that is, Moab and the sons of Ammon, of whom we said above: They will be as Sodom and Gomorrah, seem indeed to themselves, in that they are not Gentiles, to have come out of Sodom and Gomorrah; but because they blaspheme the people of God and act against Israel, they will be reckoned as Sodom and Gomorrah; and they will be blotted out as those were blotted out before, having in themselves no trace of greenness and life. Nor is it surprising if we understand this of heretics, that they are reckoned as Sodom and Gomorrah, since even to churchmen who have not observed the commandments of God and have gone out from his precepts it is said through Isaiah: Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom, and attend to the law of the Lord, people of Gomorrah. And to the elders who desire, under the figure of Susanna, to corrupt the chastity of the Church, Daniel may say: This is the judgment of God, seed of Canaan, and not of Judah. And that you may know that whenever Sodom and Gomorrah and Egypt are named, it is not said of these provinces which we see with our eyes but of other, spiritual ones, which the prophetic word threatens, read in the Apocalypse of John: But the place in which the Lord was crucified is called spiritually Sodom and Egypt. If, then, Jerusalem, in which the Lord was crucified, is called spiritually Sodom and Egypt, why should not, conversely, Egypt and Sodom and Gomorrah, if they have done the works of Jerusalem and of the land of Judah, be transferred into the land of the Lord's lot? Indeed David too was not of the priests, nor was it lawful for him to eat the loaves of proposition; but because he grew through his works one by one, and the persecution of Saul was the advancement of his virtues, therefore in his flight, without knowing it, he is suddenly made a prelate, and receives the loaves of proposition, and does not violate the commandment of God. We have said all this because Moab will be as Sodom, and the sons of Ammon as Gomorrah. Damascus too, which is interpreted drinking blood, or blood of sackcloth, will be left by the mercy of God like a heap of salt. For because its ruler is King Aretas, and the Damascenes desire to kill Paul, and he is let down through the wall in a basket, it is not said to Damascus: You are the salt of the world; nor is it called that salt which is always offered with the sacrifices, but the salt that has lost its savor, of which it is written in the Gospel: But if the salt has lost its savor, with what will it be salted? It is useful for nothing, neither for the earth nor for the dunghill, but they cast it out, so that it may be trodden underfoot by men.
Commentary on Zephaniah

And this will befall them for their pride, because they blasphemed and were magnified against the people of the Lord of hosts; and this Lord of hosts will be terrible over them, and his terror will not kill the proud; he will not shed the blood of the blasphemers, but will destroy and waste away all their idols, so that those who before were held by error and did not perceive the benefits of the Lord, pressed by the necessity of evils, may know that idols profit nothing, and may worship him, each one from his place, all the islands of the nations. Thus far according to the Hebrew.
Homily 24, on Psalm 96

But let us also call the churches islands. And indeed it is said in another place too: "Many islands shall be converted to me." Do you wish to know that the churches are called islands? It is said in the prophet in the person of the Lord: "Speak," he says, "to the inhabitants of this island." Let the many islands be glad. For just as islands are set in the midst of the sea, so also the churches are set as it were in the midst of the sea of this world, and thus they are battered by persecutions as if by diverse waves. But these islands are battered daily, yet they are not overthrown. They are indeed in the sea, but they have Christ for their foundation, who cannot be moved.
Commentary on Zephaniah

The Lord Almighty will therefore come and will be manifest over them, he whom they do not now know, of whom they are ignorant; and he will destroy all their doctrines, that is, their gods, and the idols of the various nations, so that, after the images which they had composed for themselves out of their own mind have been overthrown, the nations may turn to the Lord, and each one in his own place may worship him whom he did not know before.
ON FAITH IN THINGS UNSEEN 4

Nor think that it was foretold that the nations should come unto some one place of God, in that it was said, "Unto Thee shall the nations come from the extremity of the earth." Understand, if you can, that unto the God of the Christians, Who is the Supreme and True God, the peoples of the nations come, not by walking but by believing. For the same thing was by another prophet thus foretold, "The Lord," saith he, "shall prevail against them, and shall utterly destroy all the gods of the nations of the earth: and all the isles of the nations shall worship Him, each man from his place." Whereas the one says, "Unto Thee all nations shall come;" this the other says, "They shall worship Him, each man from his place." Therefore they shall come unto Him, not departing from their own place, because believing in Him they shall find Him in their hearts.
Commentary on Zephaniah

But if we note that in all the Scriptures those are called Ethiopians who are sunk deep in vices, according to what we read in Jeremiah: If the Ethiopian will change his skin, then, when the Ethiopians are converted to better things, there will be hope that no one who is willing to repent will be a stranger to salvation. Hence also the soul, at first polluted and stained with the filth of sins, says: I am black. And afterwards, at the end of the Song of Songs, it is written of that same soul, now cleansed and washed through repentance: Who is this who comes up made white; Moses too, that is, the spiritual law of the Lord, took to wife the Ethiopian woman from the nations. And Miriam, that is, the synagogue of the Jews, and Aaron, that is, the carnal priesthood, and not according to the order of Melchizedek, murmur against the law, but in vain. For at once the synagogue is drenched with leprosy, and, cast out of the camp, when the time is completed, at the prayer of Moses himself, she is brought back into the camp. For Ethiopia's hand had already come before God. So now the divine word threatens those who, clinging to sins and smeared with the filth of their sins, are unwilling to be converted to better things and to wash out their dark color; and it threatens them with the sword of which I think it is written also in Genesis: He set the Cherubim, and a flaming sword, which turns about to guard the way of the tree of life, and in Isaiah: He will bring a great and holy sword upon the dragon, the twisting serpent, and will kill it on that day. And he says that they will be either wounded or slain by the sword, so that, fearing the punishments, they may imitate Nineveh, and repent, and not undergo what the Lord threatens. This indeed is what the prophecy of Jeremiah also declares: I will speak, he says, concerning a nation and concerning a kingdom, and I will remove and destroy them; and if they repent, I too will repent of all the evils that I spoke of doing to them. And that you may know that the Lord now threatens the Ethiopians with the sword for this reason, that he may convert them to better things, a little later in this very book he adds concerning the Ethiopians: Beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, from there my suppliants, the daughter of my dispersed ones, will bring a gift to me, or, as it stands in the LXX: From the ends of the rivers of Ethiopia I will receive my dispersed ones, and they will offer victims to me.
Commentary on Zephaniah

But you also, Ethiopians, will be slain by my sword; and he will stretch out his hand over the north and will destroy Asshur; and he will make the beautiful one a wilderness, and a pathless place, and as it were a desert. And flocks will lie down in the midst of her, all the beasts of the nations, and the pelican and the hedgehog will dwell on her thresholds; the voice of one singing in the window, the raven on the lintel, because I will wear away her strength. This is the glorious city, dwelling in confidence, which said in her heart: I am, and outside me there is no other any more; how has she been made a desert, a lair of beasts? Everyone who passes through her will hiss and will move his hand. LXX: And you, Ethiopians, will be wounded by my sword; and I will stretch out my hand over the north and I will destroy the Assyrian; and I will make Nineveh a wilderness, and waterless as a desert. And flocks will feed in the midst of her, and all the beasts of the earth; and chameleons and hedgehogs will lie down in her stalls, and beasts will cry out in their pits, and ravens in her gates, because her height is a cedar; this is the city given over to evils, which dwells in hope, which says in her heart: I am, and there is none after me any more, how has she been made a wilderness, a pasture of beasts? Everyone who passes through her will hiss and will move his hands. The Jews refer this whole section, and the two preceding ones against the Philistines and Moab and the sons of Ammon, to the coming of Christ, who they think will come at the consummation of the world, to build up Jerusalem and to free his people from the hand of the nations by which they are held; and they say that this is the meaning of what is said: And men will worship him from their own place, all the islands of the nations. And not only the nations above, they hold, but also the Ethiopians and the Assyrians and Nineveh, the city of the Assyrians, are at that time to be made a wilderness, and all the beasts of the earth will lie down in her, or, as is written in the Hebrew, all the beasts of the nations, by which they think all the peoples that are to overthrow Nineveh are signified. And because Nineveh means beautiful, in the present passage they refer the beautiful one to Babylon. And all that follows, The pelican and the hedgehog will dwell on her thresholds, and so on, they say suits Babylon rather, whose same desolation is foretold in Isaiah also. Others, on the contrary, affirm that it is clearly said of the Assyrian, of whom it had already gone before: And he will stretch out his hand over the north, and will destroy Asshur, and will make Nineveh a wilderness. For by the Assyrians Nineveh is meant rather than Babylon, which is a city of the Chaldeans. And as for his saying, the pelican and the hedgehog in its hinges, and the raven on the lintel, these are signs of desolation; and there are two kinds of pelicans: one of the water, the other of the wilderness. And by what he says, The voice of one singing in the window, either demons are meant, or the voices of various birds that are wont to dwell in deserted cities. Moreover, where both we and the LXX have translated alike, The raven on the lintel, in the Hebrew is set hareb, which, according to a difference of reading, is taken as either dryness, or sword, or raven. Hence Aquila translated sword, and others dryness. And after the overthrow, as if mocking her ruin, the prophetic word speaks: This is the glorious city, dwelling in confidence, which said in her heart: I am, and outside me there is no other any more; how has she been made a desert, a lair of beasts? Everyone who passes through her will hiss and will move his hand. But according to what we said above, either beasts will truly dwell in the deserted city, or at any rate under the figure of beasts the variety of many nations is indicated. If anyone should ask how, according to the history, this prophecy is referred to the times of Nebuchadnezzar, when the Ethiopians and the Assyrians are also named, to whom the Medes and Persians did nothing, let him read the histories, and he will see that the Assyrians too and the Ethiopians were subject to the Medes, and he will see the reign of Cambyses, and the power of Cyrus, and all that followed thereafter. Let these things have been said in the Jewish way.
Commentary on Zephaniah

After this it is not the Lord who speaks, as above, but the prophetic spirit speaks about him: And he will stretch out his hand over the north, and will destroy Asshur. The north, of which Jeremiah wrote: From the north evils will blaze up upon all the inhabitants of the earth. And of which Solomon makes mention: The north wind is a harsh wind, but by name it is called the right. And God stretches out his hand, the hand that inflicts punishments, for this reason: that both the north may feel the penalties, and those who are in its land, to which, according to Zechariah, the black horses go, of which it is said: There were black horses, they were going into the land of the north. And fittingly, whoever has moved his feet and withdrawn from the East, of which the same prophet says: Behold a man, the East is his name, and has looked toward the west, goes at once toward the north, which is not the right, but by name is called the right. This indeed is understood bodily as well: whoever stands in the east and turns himself, looking toward the west, has the north on his right; those who have grown cold from its blast call it the right, though it is the right only in name, but in reality and in deed is rather on the left. And after the Lord has stretched out his hand over the north, he will also destroy Asshur, which means εὐθύνων, which many think means one who directs, but that is false; for εὐθύνων means one who reproves and convicts. And since the devil himself is the enemy and the avenger, and he himself suggests sins, and afterwards convicts sinners in their sins, for that reason he is called εὐθύνων. I reckon him to be the prince of the Assyrians, who dwells toward the north, and has Nineveh as his capital, and says in Isaiah: By strength I will act, and by the wisdom of understanding I will take away the boundaries of the nations, and I will devour their strength.
Commentary on Zephaniah

Moreover, what follows about Nineveh laid waste: And flocks will feed in her, and all the beasts of the earth, chameleons, and hedgehogs will lie down in her stalls, and beasts will rest in her hinges, and ravens in her windows, and so on, seems to me to have to be understood in accordance with what is written either in Jonah or in the prophet Nahum. And in Jonah indeed we interpreted Nineveh, that is, the beautiful one, which repented at the preaching of Jonah, that is, of the dove, as the Church gathered from the nations. In Nahum, however, we tempered the interpretation toward the world; and concerning the world, indeed, it is not difficult to interpret and to say that, when the Ethiopians have been wounded by the sword of the Lord, and he has stretched out his hand over the north, and has destroyed the Assyrian, the prince of the world, the world itself too perishes with its prince, and is reduced to the utmost desolation, and is pitiable to no one, but all hiss at its ruin and move their hands. But concerning the Church it seems at first sight to be blasphemous that she should become pathless and deserted, and that beasts should dwell in her, and that afterwards it should be said to her with mockery: This is the city given over to evils, which dwelt in hope, which said in her heart: I am, and there is none besides me any more, how has she been made a wilderness, a pasture of beasts? But whoever has considered that apostolic saying in which it is said: In the last times very evil times will set in, and men will be lovers of themselves, greedy, arrogant, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, without affection, without peace, accusers, intemperate, cruel, hating the good, traitors, rash, puffed up, lovers of pleasures more than of God; having the form of piety, but denying its power. And also this, which is written in the Gospel, that as iniquity is multiplied the love of many grows cold, so much so that at that time this is fulfilled: Yet when the Son of man comes, do you think he will find faith on the earth? He will not wonder at the final devastation of the Church: that, while the Antichrist reigns, she is to be reduced to a wilderness, and handed over to beasts, and is to suffer whatever the prophet now describes. For if God, because of unbelief, did not spare the natural branches, but broke them off, and turned rivers into a desert, and springs of waters into thirst, a fruitful land into saltness, because of the wickedness of its inhabitants, why should he not, conversely, overthrow those of whom he had said: He turned a desert into pools of waters, and a land without water into springs of waters, and made the hungry dwell there, and so on, and those whom he grafted from the wild olive into the root of the good olive, if, unmindful of his kindness, they withdraw from their Creator and worship the Assyrian, and bring them back to the same thirst in which they had been before? Although this can be understood generally of the coming of the Antichrist, or of the end of the world, yet it can be taken daily of those who pretend to be of the Church of God and deny it by their works, and are hearers of the law and not doers, who vainly boast that they are beautiful, when flocks dwell in them, namely a multitude of vices, and brute animals serving the body; and all the beasts of the earth, which devour their hearts, and chameleons, which do not have one color, but are changed from moment to moment by different sins, now by avarice, now by luxury, now by cruelty, now by lust, now by sadness, now by exultation. And hedgehogs in their stalls, an animal spiny and full of thorns, and wounding whatever it touches. But beasts too will lie down in the holes, that is, in their hearts, and ravens, unclean birds, in their gates, either in the mouth or in the ears, so that they may always either speak or hear evil things. After this it is added and said: the Church will suffer these things, or has suffered them, for this reason, that she raised herself up in pride and, like a cedar, lifted up her top, given over to evil works, and nonetheless promising herself future blessedness, and despising the rest in her heart, and not thinking that anyone exists besides herself, and saying: I am, and there is no other besides me any more; how then has she been made in the wilderness a pasture of beasts? For where previously the Father dwelt, and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and his angels presided over its ministries, there beasts will then dwell, about which the prophet too laments, saying: Do not hand over to the beasts the soul that confesses to you.
Commentary on Zephaniah

Everyone who passes through her will hiss and will move his hands. But if we understand this of the angels, we will interpret it thus: when the angels pass through her, and do not remain in her, as they had been accustomed to do before, they will be stunned and will marvel, and will not prop her up nor hold her up with their hand as she falls, but will lift up their hands and pass on through. Or else with a hiss they will raise their hands, and, as though lamenting in the manner of mourners, they will clap them together. If, however, we wish to take this of the devil and his angels, who also laid waste the vine that had been transplanted out of Egypt, we will say that through the soul from which Christ has withdrawn, and which before had been the temple of God and has ceased to be so, the serpent passes, and hisses in it, and vomits out the venoms of his malice, and not only does this, but also moves his works, which τροπικῶς (figuratively) are called hands. And lest you think, because we have named a serpent, that we forcibly understand the hands of a serpent as its work, take the testimony of Solomon: Death and life are in the hands of the tongue. We have said these things serving the allegorical interpretation as best we could. But if anyone finds things more probable and more reasonable than those set out by us, let the reader rather be led by his authority.

n: Dove. Jerusalem is upbraided, and then comforted. She had been treated like a spouse, a dove; and yet proved faithless. (Calmet) --- Hebrew, "Woe to the famous, and defiled, and oppressing city." Septuagint agree with us, if we only exchange famous for provoking. (Haydock) --- After being redeemed from Egypt, the Jews ungratefully follow idols, Osee vii. 11. (Menochius) --- Jerusalem having been freely chosen and favoured above other places, and still provoking God, cannot escape a severe chastisement. (Worthington)
Lord. She had recourse rather to the princes of Assyria and of Egypt, which proved her ruin.
Evening. Septuagint, "Arabian," Habacuc i. 8. Such was the state of the kingdom before the reform of Josias. (Calmet)
Senseless. Protestants, "light," or (Haydock) windy and inconstant. There were too many false prophets (Calmet) during the minority of Josias. (Haydock)

Morning. Speedily he will punish the guilty before all. --- Shame. He is hardened. (Calmet) --- Septuagint, "and not injustice for victory." Grabe substitutes contention. God is just, (Haydock) even when he takes vengeance. (Calmet)
Towers. Literally, "angles," (Haydock) the chiefs, or to the very last, Job xxxviii. 6., and Zacharias x. 4. The nations have been punished for an example. But you do not take warning. (Calmet)

But. Septuagint, "be prepared, rise early, all their grapes are corrupt." (Haydock) --- I had reason to expect an amendment, when so many nations had perished before their eyes. (Calmet) --- They however sinned out of malice, and strove to provoke me in all their ways.

To come. Septuagint, "for a witness." (Haydock) --- About forty years after Christ's resurrection, the Jews for the most part continuing obstinate, Titus ruined their city; which is a figure of the world's destruction, and of the eternal punishment of the wicked. (Worthington) --- After the resurrection, the Church was to be gathered from all nations. Christ will rise again at the last day to judge all. God threatens his rebellious people with captivity, and then promises to shew mercy, ver. 9. Thus the prophets often subjoin promises to threats.

Chosen. Symmachus, "pure." (Calmet) --- Idols shall not be mentioned. (Theodoret) --- All people shall know and adore the Lord, which was verified only after Christ's coming. (Calmet) --- Septuagint, "for then I will change again for the peoples, language to its own kind," (Haydock) which Origen, (contra Cels. viii.) and the Jews in St. Jerome, explain of the days of the Messias, when the confusion of Babel shall cease. But this is forced: it suffices that people unite in faith and obey the Church. --- Shoulder, like people carrying a burden. Septuagint, "under one yoke." After the captivity the Jews were more obedient and faithful, as the more corrupt remained behind the Euphrates, or were cut off in the last wars. Yet the synagogue was never so pure as the Christian Church, even in the worst times. (Calmet) --- All nations shall worship God in unity of faith, and courageously submit to the gospel. (Worthington)

Ethiopia. The Nile arises in that country, and runs through Egypt and Arabia, which is often styled Ethiopia or Cush, Isaias xviii. 1. The Jews came from Egypt to adore at Jerusalem, even after the building of Onion. Yet this literally regards Christ's Church. --- Offering. The Jews performed this after the captivity, coming or sending the half sicle to Jerusalem annually, from all quarters of the world, Numbers iii. 46., and Matthew xvii. 23. (Calmet)

Doings. Literally, "inventions," of religion of thy own choice. (Haydock) --- Thy past offenses shall be obliterated, and thou shalt commit nothing of the kind any more. Those proud spirits who caused thee to dislike my law, and who set up idols in my temple shall disappear. --- Mountain. The temple shall be destroyed, that all may know that I am attached to virtue alone, (Calmet) and not to any edifice or place. (Haydock) --- They trusted too much to the temple, Jeremias vii. 4. (Menochius)

Poor in spirit. (Haydock) --- Hebrew, "meek and extenuated," who trust not in themselves. This is the character of true Christians. The few Jews who remained in the country, or who returned from Babylon, might well represent them, being poor and dependent. The disciples of Christ contemned riches, and were resolute only where virtue was at stake. (Calmet) --- They were instructed by poor fishermen taught by God. (Menochius)

Israel. They shall be more submissive, and afraid of yielding to idolatry. Yet the synagogue was far from the perfection of primitive Christianity, or even from that of many pious souls in these days of relaxation. --- Afraid. The Jews were not much molested till the time of Epiphanes, nor was the country ravaged as it had been, Micheas ii. 12. This peace is however of a spiritual nature, granted by Christ to those who fight against their passions, John xiv. 27. (Calmet) --- They shall feed on the word of God and on the blessed Eucharist. (Menochius)

Judgment, or "condemnation." Septuagint, "iniquities," (Calmet) nailing to the cross the handwriting that was against thee. (Haydock) --- God does not treat thee with rigour. He will be thy king. The Jews had no king for a long time. But the true Israel, of whom the prophet speaks, is continually ruled and fed by Jesus Christ, who imparts his graces abundantly. (Calmet)

Silent; constant. (Menochius) --- He will accuse thee no more. Can this be understood of the Jews, who have been cast off till the fulness of the Gentiles enter the Church? [Romans xi. 25.] To the latter all this must be applied. Few prophets inveighed against the crimes of the captives after their return. (Calmet) --- But this must be deemed a punishment, unless the crimes were also removed. (Haydock)

Triflers. Literally, "trifles;" nugas. Hebrew nugi, (Haydock) which is almost Latin. (St. Jerome) --- These vain nothings, (Calmet) men who were of light dispositions, scoffers at Christ, shall be converted and honour him. (Worthington) --- Septuagint, 17. "he will renew thee in his love, and will exult over thee in joy, as on a festival day: (18) and I will bring back thy bruised ones. Woe to him that has reproached her." Aquila likewise renders by woe, or eju, oh, oi, using it as an exclamation, though not of sorrow. Yet the term signifies, they were. (St. Jerome) (Haydock) --- Hebrew literally, "I have gathered those who were in grief for a time. They were of thee. Shame was upon them like a heavy load;" or, "they were grieved on account of the festivals disused. They were like an offering rejected," with disgrace. (Calmet) --- They lamented that they could no longer observe the solemn festivals, and this was to the pious a most intolerable burden, while libertines seem to feel as great a misery in the observance.

Cut. Septuagint, "do in thee, for thy sake at," &c. (Haydock) --- Halteth, and have no children, (Micheas iv. 7.) denoting the Gentiles. (Calmet) --- Septuagint, "squeezed out," like grapes, being in distress. (St. Jerome) --- Where. Septuagint, "and they shall be ashamed at," &c.

Bring. Septuagint, "do good to you." (Haydock) --- Praise. All shall speak well of you who have been lately dishonoured, when I shall take both Gentiles and Jews for my spouse after the captivity, which seems present, (Calmet) it is so certain. (Haydock) --- Captivity, under satan and sin. (Menochius)

f: Commentary on Zephaniah

Woe, provoking and redeemed city, the dove. She did not hear the voice, and did not accept discipline; she did not trust in the Lord, she did not draw near to her Lord. Her princes in the midst of her, like roaring lions; her judges, wolves of the evening, they left nothing for the morning. Her prophets mad, faithless men. Her priests have polluted the holy, they have acted unjustly against the law. The just Lord in the midst of her will not do iniquity. In the morning, in the morning he will give his judgment in the light, and it will not be hidden; but the unjust one knew no confusion. I have destroyed the nations, and their corners have been scattered; I have made their ways deserted, because there is no one who passes; their cities have been made desolate, with no man remaining, nor any inhabitant. I said: Yet you will fear me, you will accept discipline, and her dwelling will not perish because of all the things in which I visited her. Nevertheless, rising at dawn, they corrupted all their thoughts. LXX: O illustrious and redeemed city, the dove, she did not hear the voice, she did not accept discipline; she did not trust in the Lord, and did not draw near to her Lord. Her princes in her like roaring lions, her judges like wolves of Arabia, they did not leave anything till the morning; her prophets bearing the spirit, men who are despisers. Her priests pollute the holy things, and act impiously against the law. But the just Lord is in the midst of her, and will not do iniquity. In the morning, in the morning he will give his judgment in the light, and he is not hidden, and he does not know iniquity in exaction, nor injustice for ever; I have pulled down the proud, their corners have been scattered, I have destroyed their ways, so that they may not pass through at all; their cities have failed, because no one remained, nor dwelt there. I said: Nevertheless you will fear me, and you will accept discipline, and you will not perish from his eyes in all the things in which I have taken vengeance upon her. Prepare yourself, rise up at dawn, all their clusters have perished. Many think that, because of the sequence of the discourse, this is said against Nineveh, of which it was said above: And he will destroy the Assyrian, and will make Nineveh a wilderness. But Scripture would never call Nineveh a dove, although some think that in Jeremiah the words from the face of the sword of the dove were said about Nebuchadnezzar. But it should be known that others, on the contrary, assert that in place of dove, Ἑλλάδα, that is, Greece, can be understood there, so that the sense is: From the face of the sword of Iona, that is, from the face of the sword of Greece. For Iona signifies both dove and Greece. Hence even to this day the Greeks are called Ionians, and the sea is called the Ionian Sea, and among the Hebrews their old name remains. So too the Roman princes, retaining an ancient name among the barbarian nations, are called Caesars. The whole discourse, then, is against Jerusalem: Woe, city once a dove, always sinning, and handed over to captivities, and redeemed again by the Lord. Woe, provoking city, which is said more expressively in Hebrew, mara, that is, παραπικραίνουσα, which we can render making God bitter, that is, by your fault turning the sweet and merciful Lord to bitterness, so that he who wishes to have mercy is compelled to punish.
Commentary on Zephaniah

But the illustrious city, redeemed by the blood of Christ, is clearly understood, in keeping with what was said above, as the Church, which is also called a dove because of the simplicity of the multitude of believers within her.
Commentary on Zephaniah

Nor let it disturb anyone, as I have often said already, that I interpret these things as spoken against the Church, since he knows that in the holy Scriptures Jerusalem always bears the type of the Church; whoever sins away from her is either led off into Babylon, or, if he chooses of his own accord to go down to Jericho, is wounded by robbers. For what is so illustrious as the Church, which has been founded in the whole world, so redeemed by the blood of Christ, and a dove because of the grace of the Holy Spirit, as the Church gathered from the nations? In her very many who say that they believe in Christ have neither heard his voice, nor received discipline, nor wished to be near him.
Commentary on Zephaniah

She did not hear the commandment of the Lord, and when rebuked she would not accept discipline; nor, when evils pressed upon her, did she ever trust in the Lord her God; nor did she walk behind him; nor, when he said: I am the Lord who draws near, and not from afar, was she herself willing to draw near to him.
Commentary on Zephaniah

She did not hear the voice of the Lord, nor was she willing to accept discipline, nor did she trust in the Lord, because she would not draw near to the Lord her God so as to merit pardon of sins. For in vain does anyone say that he hears the voice of the Lord his God and trusts in the Lord, when he destroys faith by his works, and is joined to mammon more than to the Lord his God, and approaches him with a double heart, and believes that he can serve as a soldier under two masters, the world and God.
Commentary on Zephaniah

Her princes are like roaring lions. We have no doubt about the roaring and the ranging of lions when we see her princes thunder so against the peoples subject to them, and crush the common people with a tyrant's voice and rabid abuse, that you would think it not a shepherd among his flock, but a lion gnashing its teeth among the little sheep. Her judges too are like wolves of Arabia, killing in the evening and leaving nothing for the morning; not looking toward the rising of the sun, but lingering always in darkness, and turning the small possessions of the Church, and the things brought as offerings to God, to their own gain, so that the poor have nothing to eat in the morning; they lay everything waste as if in the night, with no one seeing; and when, after the manner of wolves, they plunder everything, they do not leave even small portions of food to the needy.
Commentary on Zephaniah

As for the saying: Her princes in her like roaring lions, I know that I will offend very many, because I interpret these things of bishops and elders, though the wicked elders who desired to violate Susanna do not condemn the other elders who have lived well. And the wicked princes whom the prophetic word describes are no reproach to good princes: For when a fool is scourged, the senseless man will be wiser; but if the senseless man becomes wiser, how much more he who is wise? But her judges and princes, taking gifts and selling justice, are they not rightly called wolves of Arabia, or evening wolves, as Symmachus translated? For they do not deserve to be called wolves of Benjamin, which seize prey in the morning and at evening give food, but evening wolves, which eat by night and leave nothing for the morning.
Commentary on Zephaniah

Her princes and judges and prophets and priests are also described, so that in the city we may understand the people, and in these titles of rank that I have mentioned, the leading men. Her princes, therefore, like lions, were always busy with plunder and with shedding the blood of their subjects; her judges were rapacious, leaving to others nothing they could seize. Her prophets, raving or astounded, which in Hebrew is said phoezim, and Aquila translated θαμβευταὶ (the astonished), spoke as if from the mouth of the Lord, and proclaimed everything against the Lord; the priests committed sacrilege in the place of the sanctuary, and while they acted against the law, they offered sacrifices according to the law.
Commentary on Zephaniah

Her prophets also, that is, the teachers who think that they teach the peoples and discourse on the Scriptures, πνευματοφόροι, that is, bearing the spirit, or spiritual — and this is to be read εἰρονικῶς (ironically) —, are men who are despisers; for what befits the Church is not to teach but to do, not to destroy words by deeds. But you, when you teach another and do not do it yourself, are to be called not so much a teacher as a despiser, of whom it is also written in Habakkuk: Look, you despisers, and behold, and wonder at the wonders, and perish. The priests too, who serve the Eucharist and distribute the blood of the Lord to his peoples, act impiously against the law of Christ, thinking that it is the words of the one who prays that make the εὐχαριστίαν (the Eucharist), not his life, and that only the solemn prayer is necessary, and not the merits of the priests, of whom it is said: And a priest in whom there is any blemish shall not approach to offer offerings to the Lord.
Commentary on Zephaniah

As for what follows: Her prophets πνευματοφόροι, that is, bearing the spirit, men who are despisers, let it disturb no one that, interpreting this of teachers, we call the same men both prophets and despisers, since the Apostle too commands: Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed in the day of redemption. And David says in Psalm 50 (51): Do not take your Holy Spirit from me. For unless the Holy Spirit, when grieved, were accustomed to flee his former lodging and to abandon his dwelling, Paul would never have commanded what I said above, nor would David after his adultery have dreaded lest he lose what he had received; of which it is also written to the Hebrews: How much worse punishments do you think he deserves who has trampled on the Son of God, and has held unclean the blood of the covenant, in which he was sanctified, and has done insult to the spirit of grace? Moreover, it is written in the third book of Kingdoms (1 Kings) that the man of God, no doubt a prophet, who had said to the altar in Samaria: Altar, altar, thus says the Lord: Behold, a son of David will be born, and so on, because he despised the words of the Lord and ate with the false prophet — for so Josephus, expounding this passage, interpreted it —, was killed by a lion. And lest it be thought chance and not the judgment of the Lord, both the false prophet who had deceived him foretold that this would happen, and the lion itself, punishing the despiser, spared the ass. It is no wonder, then, if teachers who had been full of the Holy Spirit can become despisers, since among the careless, who do not keep their heart with all watchfulness, this very thing is frequently the cause of pride against the Lord and of contempt: that they have the knowledge of God, and know his great goodness, which he has hidden for those who fear him, and despise the riches of his goodness, storing up for themselves wrath in the day of wrath and of revelation. Let the priests too — who give baptism and at the Eucharist pray for the coming of the Lord, make the oil of chrism, lay on hands, instruct catechumens, appoint Levites and other priests — not so much be indignant with us for expounding these things, and with the prophets for prophesying them, as pray to the Lord, and take earnest care that they may not deserve to be among the priests who violate the holy things of the Lord. For it is not rank and the names of rank, but the work of the rank, that is accustomed to save princes, and judges, and prophets, and priests: He who desires the episcopate, he says, desires a good work. See what he said: He desires a good work, not a rank. But if, despising the work, one looks only at the rank, swiftly the tower in Siloam falls, and the heights of the cedar are struck by lightning, and the upraised neck is broken, and the swan, with neck outstretched and straining aloft, is reckoned among the unclean birds.
Commentary on Zephaniah

Therefore, because they acted unjustly, the just Lord will not do iniquity, but will render to the most wicked city what it deserves. In the morning, in the morning, that is, openly and without any ambiguity, he will pass judgment on her, and there will be nothing that can be hidden from him. And the Lord will do this so that the city, rebuked, may be converted to the better. But unjust Israel did not recognize its confusion, nor did it understand that the blows were inflicted on it for this purpose, that it might repent.
Commentary on Zephaniah

Though the princes, judges, prophets, priests of Jerusalem do these things, the Lord is nonetheless merciful and just. Merciful, in that he does not withdraw from his Church; just, in that he renders to each one what he deserves. For after the morning has come, and the night of this age has passed, he will give his judgment in the light, and neither he himself nor his judgment will be hidden.
Commentary on Zephaniah

And when he begins to demand from each one the money he had entrusted to them, he will not be unjust, nor will he make injustice prevail for ever, but he will pull down the proud princes, whom God resists, from their seats and from the height they held, and their corners will be scattered, that is, their perverse wills, turning aside from the straight road, corners in which the Pharisees too were always accustomed to pray, having despised the corner stone. But I think that it benefits the proud too to be pulled down from their arrogance, and to have their alleys and corners scattered, so that afterwards they may walk on the straight road. Then follows: And I will make their ways deserted, because there is no one who passes through, according to what is written in Psalm 1: And the way of the impious will perish. And also in Hosea, where it is said of Jerusalem committing fornication: Behold, I will close her ways with thorns, and I will block up her paths, and she will not find her track, and she will pursue her lovers, and will not overtake them, and she will seek them, and will not find them; and she will say: I will go and return to my former husband, for it was better with me then than now. Notice that unless the ways had been closed and the paths fenced off, and unless the Lord had destroyed her ways, the fornicating soul could never have said: I will go and return to my former husband. So the paths of the proud and their corners are scattered, that they may not walk in pride and in perversity, and their cities, which had been wickedly built in arrogance and pride, are destroyed, so that they may not stand and have most wicked inhabitants.
Commentary on Zephaniah

I have avenged you, he says afterwards, on the nations, and I have destroyed their empires, so that you who had not perceived me through blows might at least know me through benefits. Or else it is to be understood thus: I have destroyed all your cities, O Judah, and all the villages and tribes subject to you, and the various borderlands, and so great was the desolation of men that there was no one to dwell in your cities; and after I did this, I sent my prophets, rising at dawn and calling to repentance, and I said: I have indeed done these things to you, O Jerusalem, but I did them that you might fear me, and accept discipline, and that your dwelling, that is, the temple, might not perish because of all the crimes you had committed. But on the contrary, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, while I was calling them to repentance, rose at dawn as if on purpose and out of contention, so that with the haste with which they ought to have returned to me they might fulfil all their thoughts, and show in deed what they had conceived in mind. This according to the Hebrew.
Commentary on Zephaniah

And lest anyone think that we do violence to Scripture, let him learn from what follows. But I did these things, he says, that I might say to them: Behold, the paths of malice have been destroyed; from now on fear me, and learn discipline, lest my discipline also perish, finding in you no fruit of conversion, and all the things by which I wished to correct you be in vain, and that word which is written in Jeremiah may be applied to you: In vain have I struck your sons; you have not accepted discipline. Or else: Fear me, and receive discipline, so that all things may not perish from the sight of Jerusalem, nor she be brought utterly to desolation over these evils with which I threatened her.
Commentary on Zephaniah

Moreover, what we have expounded according to the Hebrew, Nevertheless, rising at dawn, they corrupted all their thoughts, in place of which it is written in the Seventy: Prepare yourself, rise up at dawn, all their foliage has been scattered, since it differs much from the Hebrew, and according to the LXX seems rather to agree with what follows, we will expound in what follows.
Commentary on Zephaniah

But we, who follow not the letter that kills but the spirit that gives life, nor Jewish fables, hear from the Lord: Prepare yourself, rise at dawn: all their clusters have been scattered, and, prepared, we say: My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready. And we hear the command in Proverbs: Prepare your works for your going out. And that which is said in a sacred manner in Leviticus, where in the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, Aaron offers for the people the scapegoat, and that a living one, and, laying his hands upon its head, calls down upon it all the sins of the people of Israel, and hands it over into the hands of a prepared man, and sends it into the desert, this we understand of ourselves, and, preparing ourselves at the command of the true priest, we remove evil from the midst of the Church. And when we have done these things, the night passes, the day draws near, and, walking honestly as in the day, we say: O God, my God, to you I keep watch from the dawn. And at once we add: In the morning you will hear my prayer, in the morning I will stand before you, and I will see. For unless we have been prepared, the sun of justice will not rise for us. But when the sun has risen, all the clusters from the vine of Sodom are scattered and perish, so that, as the lamp of Christ shines, not only the great bunches but even what seemed to be small in us perishes.
Commentary on Zephaniah

Therefore wait for me, says the Lord, on the day of my resurrection in the future; for my judgment is to gather the nations and to collect the kingdoms, to pour out upon them my indignation, all the wrath of my fury; for in the fire of my zeal all the earth will be devoured, because then I will restore to the peoples a chosen lip, that all may call upon the name of the Lord and serve him with one shoulder. LXX: Therefore wait for me, says the Lord, on the day of my resurrection for a testimony, for my judgment is upon the gatherings of the nations, that I may receive kings, that I may pour out upon them all my wrath, the wrath of my fury; for in the fire of my zeal all the earth will be consumed, for then I will turn among the peoples a tongue into its generations, that all may call upon the name of the Lord, that they may serve him under one yoke. The Jews interpret these things of the coming of Christ, whom they hope is yet to come, and they say that, when all the nations have been gathered and the fury of the Lord has been poured out upon them, the earth will be devoured in the fire of his zeal. And just as before the building of the tower there was a time when all peoples spoke one tongue, so, when all have been converted to the worship of the true God, they will speak Hebrew and the whole world will serve the Lord.
Commentary on Zephaniah

It should be noted, however, that in the place where we translated: I will restore to the peoples a chosen lip, instead of chosen the Seventy said: into its generation, so that of the earth is to be understood. And the error arose from this, that the Hebrew word barura, which Aquila and Theodotion translated as chosen and Symmachus as pure, the Seventy read as badura, thinking the letter res (resh) to be daleth, because of the excessive similarity of the character, which is distinguished by a small stroke. And likewise, where we translated: On the day of my resurrection in the future, all the others too translated: for a testimony. The Hebrew who instructed me in the Scriptures maintained that laed in the present passage ought to be understood rather as εἰς ἔτι, that is, for the future, than as for a testimony. For Ed, which is written with the letters ain and daleth, is understood as ἔτι and μαρτύριον, that is, both the future and a testimony. We can also expound this passage of the first coming of Christ, when, all error having been removed, the demons trampled and earthly works destroyed, the apostles spoke in all tongues, and, the old error having been removed, the one lip of confession was restored. But the kings, too, who are destroyed and consumed by the divine burning, are to be understood as the leaders of perverse doctrines.
Commentary on Zephaniah

And, promising us a reward for all these things, God says: Wait for me on the day of my resurrection for a testimony; for after vices and sins God will rise again in us. And according to what he commands in another place: Be my witnesses, and I am a witness, says the Lord God, and the servant whom I have chosen, the Father with the Son and the Holy Spirit is a witness for us, so that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may stand. And it seems to me that the sentence stands rather in this way, and that the truth is confirmed under these three witnesses, rather than through the letter. For there were two witnesses against Susanna, and against the Lord Savior himself, and yet the word did not stand in their mouth. Against Naboth, too, almost the whole city bore witness, and the agreement of most wicked witnesses had not the firmness of truth but the conspiracy of a crime. For my judgment, he says, is upon the gatherings of the nations, that I may receive kings, namely in the place of their punishments, that I may pour out upon them my wrath, all the wrath of my fury. He who is lesser quickly earns pardon and is very near to mercy: But the mighty will suffer torments mightily. Hence the nations and the multitude of the nations are gathered to judgment; but the kings, that is, the leaders of perverse doctrines, will be brought to punishment, so that all the wrath of the Lord's fury may be poured out upon them. And this is done not out of any cruelty, as the bloodthirsty Jews suppose, but out of mercy and the counsel of one who heals. For there follows: For in the fire of my zeal all the earth will be consumed. For when the nations have been gathered to judgment, and the kings to punishment, so that wrath may be poured out upon them, and not in part but whole, and with wrath and fury joined together, whatever is earthly in the whole world may be consumed, whatever pertains to the works of the earth, that is, of the flesh; laying waste all its brambles and thorny thickets, the blaze of my zeal will devour it.
Commentary on Zephaniah

And then I will turn upon the peoples a tongue into its generation, so that each one, having laid aside error, may return to the ancient speech of confessing the Lord, and at the name of Jesus every knee shall bend, of those in heaven, on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess the Lord Jesus in the glory of God the Father. And casting away the bricks and the bitumen which we had in place of stones and clay, with which we were building up the pride of our error against the Lord, let us recover the tongue which we lost before, and let us be under the yoke of Christ, who says: My yoke is sweet, and my burden is light.
Morals on the Book of Job, Book 21.33

Because bodily action is carried on by the shoulder and the arm, if the good things which he put forth with the lips he did not fulfil in deed, he wishes to himself 'the shoulder to fall,' and 'the arm to be broken in pieces.' As though he said in plain words, 'If the things that I said I refused to do, this very member of my body, which was given to me for working withal, may I lose, that surely that may fall from the body which I would not exercise to advantage.' But if this sentence of a curse is to be referred to a spiritual meaning, it is doubtless plain that the arm is joined to the body by the shoulders, and as by the arm good practice, so by the shoulder the knitting together of social life, is denoted. Whence too the Prophet, regarding the holy peoples of the Church universal, that should serve God in concord, says, And they shall serve Him with one shoulder.
Commentary on Zephaniah

Beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, from there my suppliants, the sons of my dispersed ones, will bring a gift to me. On that day you will not be confounded over all your devices by which you have transgressed against me; for then I will take away from your midst the boastful ones of your pride, and you will no more be exalted on my holy mountain. And I will leave in your midst a poor and needy people, and they will hope in the name of the Lord. The remnant of Israel will not do iniquity, nor speak a lie; and a deceitful tongue will not be found in their mouth, for they will feed and lie down, and there will be none to terrify. LXX: From the ends of the rivers of Ethiopia I will receive my dispersed ones; they will bring sacrifices to me. On that day you will not be confounded by all your devices by which you have acted impiously against me, for then I will take away from you the disparagement of your insolence, and you will no more be magnified upon my holy mountain; and I will leave in you a meek and humble people, and those who are left of Israel will revere the name of the Lord, and they will not do iniquity; and they will not speak vain things, and a deceitful tongue will not be found in their mouth, for they will feed and lie down, and there will be none to terrify them. When the Lord has restored to the peoples of believers a chosen lip, and all have called upon the name of the Lord and have carried his yoke, then also from beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, whence the queen of Sheba came to hear the wisdom of Solomon, they will bring sacrifices to the Lord: And Ethiopia will hasten her hand to God; and the Ethiopian woman will be married to the true lawgiver, who struck Egypt with ten plagues, while the synagogue of the Hebrews envies. But what he says according to the Hebrew: From there my suppliants, the daughter of my dispersed ones, will bring a gift to me, is of this kind: O Israel, O synagogue, once a daughter, whom I dispersed through the whole world, though you envy, though you are tormented by jealousy, nevertheless sacrifices will be brought to me from Ethiopia, that is, from the people of the Gentiles.
Commentary on Zephaniah

But we, taking from this fable the occasion of a true history, will say that, once a chosen lip, or a pure and white one, as Symmachus translated, has been restored to us, we leave behind in the rivers of Ethiopia all the blackness of the soul, and the foul colour, and the venom of the dragon, with which we had been dyed by vices and sins, and the masters of perverse doctrines by whom we were formerly watered, and that we, with the once-dispersed Israel, will bring gifts to Christ.
Commentary on Zephaniah

On that day, that is, when the multitude of the nations has believed, you too will not be utterly confounded over all your errors by which you transgressed against me, by choosing Barabbas and crucifying the Son of God. Then I will take away from your midst the scribes and priests and Pharisees, the boastful ones of your pride, and you will by no means boast any longer on my holy mountain, but you will have a poor people, unlettered men and fishermen, who will hope in the name of the Lord.
Commentary on Zephaniah

On that day, on which the light of Christ has risen for us, it will be said to each one of us: You will not be confounded by all your devices, namely the most wicked thoughts by which we acted impiously against the Lord; and all the pride and insolence will be taken away through which we were raised up against the Lord and against the mountain, his holy one, our Lord and Savior; and in place of proud and vain names a meek and humble people will be left in us, so that we may think nothing arrogant, nothing swollen, nothing that displeases God. And at the same time consider that on the day of judgment and in the consummation of the world all the names of dignities will be taken away, and one people will remain, and a flock under the good shepherd, which is meek and humble.
Commentary on Zephaniah

The remnant of Israel, not the multitude that cried out: Crucify, crucify him, not the high priests and the nobles, but the remnant, will by no means do iniquity, nor speak a lie in Christ, since they believe the truth; nor will a deceitful tongue be found in their mouth, since they know that every lie is from the devil; for they will feed and will say: The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture, there he has set me. Beside the water of refreshment he has brought me up; he has turned my soul; and there will be none to terrify, as the faith of believers overcomes the pride of persecutors. Let this be understood of the first coming of Christ, which the Jews promise themselves at the end; and they hope that they will dwell in Jerusalem, and, after the manner of cattle, will be filled with the bodily gifts and riches of Judah and fed on green grass, and that, when all the nations have been destroyed and made subject to them, no one can remain who might terrify them.
Commentary on Zephaniah

Then also the people of Israel, when the fullness of the nations has come in, for God has shut up all under sin, that he may have mercy on all, will fear the name of the Lord. And the remnant of Israel will no longer do the iniquity through which they denied the Lord, nor speak vain things, promising themselves foolish fables; nor will a tongue of lying be found in their mouth, since Christ, who is the truth, speaks through them. For then they too will feed in one flock, and will lie down in the Church, and will not fear the onslaughts of the true Nebuchadnezzar. Seeing and reading these things, such great mysteries, let us cry out with the Apostle and say: O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God, how inscrutable are your judgments, and your ways unsearchable. The prophet, too, perceiving this and turning it over within himself, conjectures concerning the judgments of God: In the night I was exercised with my heart, and I swept my spirit, and I was saying: Will God cast off for ever, or will he not add to have mercy any more, or will he hold back his mercies in his wrath? And I said: Now I have begun; this is the change of the right hand of the Most High. And the sense is: This, that I thought the Lord was abandoning sinners for ever and, with wrath taking its place, restraining his mercies, I understood to have been done for this reason, that by the change of his right hand, which is the right hand of the Most High, he might change all things and have mercy on those whom he had previously cast away. Therefore let us also, both we and the remnant of Israel, knowing that we are to render an account for every idle word, and that the Lord will destroy all lying lips, not speak vanity. For vanity of vanities, and all is vanity, and: Every living man is utter vanity. Nor let us bring forth a lie with our mouth, but, having received the power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and upon all the power of the enemy, let us fear no terror, nor, with Christ as our guardian, dread the snares of wolves, but let us say: The Lord is my illumination and my savior; whom shall I fear? and the rest that is contained in Psalm 26 (27).
Catechetical Lecture 3:16

Take heart, O Jerusalem, the Lord will take away your iniquities. The Lord will wash away the filth of his sons and daughters by the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning. He will pour upon you clean water, and you shall be cleansed from all your sins. Choiring angels shall encircle you, chanting, "Who is it that comes up all white and leaning upon her beloved?"
