For the soul that was formerly a slave has now accounted its Lord as its kinsman, and he, acknowledging its sincere purpose, will answer, "Ah, you are beautiful, my beloved, ah, you are beautiful … your teeth are like a flock of ewes to be shorn"—a sincere confession is a spiritual shearing. And further: "all of them big with twins," signifying the twofold grace, either that perfected by water and the Spirit or that announced in the Old and in the New Testament. God grant that all of you, your course of fasting finished, mindful of the teaching, fruitful in good works, standing blameless before the spiritual bridegroom, may obtain the remission of your sins from God, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be the glory forever and ever. Amen.
Commentary on Zephaniah

Praise, daughter of Zion, shout for joy, Israel; be glad and exult with all your heart, daughter of Jerusalem. The Lord has taken away your judgment, he has turned away your enemies; the King of Israel, the Lord, is in your midst; you will not fear evil any more. On that day it will be said: Jerusalem, do not fear, Zion; let your hands not be weakened. The Lord your God in your midst, the mighty one, he will save; he will rejoice over you with gladness, he will be silent in his love for you; he will exult over you with praise. Triflers (nugas) who withdrew from the law I will gather, because they were of you, so that you may no longer have reproach over them. LXX: Rejoice, daughter of Zion; proclaim, daughter of Jerusalem; exult and delight with all your heart, daughter of Jerusalem. The Lord has taken away your iniquities, he has redeemed you from the hands of your enemies; the King of Israel, the Lord, is in your midst; you will not see evils any more. At that time the Lord says to Jerusalem: Take courage, Zion, let your hands not be weakened. The Lord your God in you, the mighty one, will save you; he will bring gladness upon you, and will renew you in his love, and will rejoice in you with delight, as on a solemn day; I will gather your broken ones. Woe to him who has taken up reproach against her. Let it not seem strange, as we have often said, that the Hebrew chapters end in one way and those of the LXX, that is, the Greek and the Latin, in another. For where the translation differs in sense, there the beginnings or the ends must also differ. The Jews promise themselves all these things together with the Christ whom they think is yet to come, things which we, who have received Christ, have already obtained together with him. If, then, any of the Christians, and especially of the new wise men, whose names I pass over in silence lest I seem to wound anyone, thinks that the prophecy has not yet been fulfilled, let him know that he bears the name of Christ falsely, and has a Jewish soul, lacking only the circumcision of the body. For if these things have not yet happened but are still to come, we have believed in the coming of the Savior in vain; but, since our believing is not in vain, we understand that the mystery has been fulfilled in us which was kept silent through eternal ages and has now been made manifest through the prophetic scriptures and the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Commentary on Zephaniah

These things, meanwhile, if we wish to take them of the second coming of the Savior. Moreover, since the prophet Zechariah exhorts Zion and Jerusalem to a similar gladness, and Matthew says that this very prophecy was fulfilled in the first coming of Christ, we are compelled by necessity, or rather led by the very order of truth, to hope for what is said in Zephaniah not as future but as done. For it is written in Zechariah: Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; proclaim, daughter of Jerusalem. Behold, your king comes to you, just and a savior, himself humble and mounted upon a beast of burden and a new colt. Let these things have been said according to the Seventy.
Commentary on Zephaniah

Finally, let us consider the order of the reading, and we shall see that what is said pertains not to the Jews but to the Church of Christ. For after what had gone before: My judgment is upon the gatherings of the nations, that I may receive kings, up to the place where he says: That all may call upon the name of the Lord, and serve him under one yoke, and: Beyond the rivers of Ethiopia I will receive among my dispersed ones those who will bring me sacrifices; and after the remnant of the people of Israel, believing in Christ and saved, of whom it is said: And those who are left of Israel will fear the name of the Lord, and there will be none to terrify them. The Holy Spirit, preaching of the general consummation of the world, speaks: Rejoice, daughter of Zion, proclaim, daughter of Jerusalem, rejoice and delight with all your heart, daughter of Jerusalem. For every soul of the Church, which is set upon the watchtower and contemplates peace, is glad and rejoices that its iniquities have been taken away from it, and redeemed by him who redeemed all with his precious blood. For Christ has been made for us wisdom from God, and justice, and sanctification, and redemption, and the King of Israel has redeemed us, who dwells in our midst, saying: I and my Father will come, and we will make our abode with him. And: I will dwell and walk among them; and we will no longer see evils, thinking and doing virtues alone.
Commentary on Zephaniah

But according to the Hebrew, the Church is commanded to praise, and Israel, seeing God with the mind, to shout for joy, and the place of peace to exult and be glad with all its heart, to which it was said: My peace I give to you, my peace I leave to you.
Commentary on Zephaniah

For at the end and in the consummation of the world he has taken away her judgment, by no means judging and rebuking her, but saving her, and he has turned away her enemies, the hosts of demons. The King of Israel, the Lord, will be in her midst; she will not fear evil any more.
Commentary on Zephaniah
On that day, says the Lord, as we see peace and are set on high, let your hands not be weakened, he who also said through Isaiah: Be strengthened, weakened hands, and let your works be strong.
Commentary on Zephaniah

On that day it will be said to Jerusalem the free, who is not in slavery with her children, but who is the mother of the saints: Do not fear, Zion, for she herself is also Jerusalem; your works will by no means be weakened, nor will you do things which you will mourn having done.
Commentary on Zephaniah

For the mighty Lord, whom no one can resist, your savior, will himself restore to you the gladness which you lost, and, the old man cast away, will make you walk in the new, and he will do these things in his love, not by your merit but by his mercy. And he will rejoice in you and delight, receiving your salvation as the richest victim of your solemnity; and he himself will say to you: I will gather your crushed ones. A heart, indeed, crushed and humbled God will not despise, and: A crushed reed he will not break.
Commentary on Zephaniah

The Lord your God, who will save you, mighty and powerful, will himself dwell in your midst; he will rejoice over you with exultation and gladness, and will keep silent about your sins in the love with which he loved you; and he will exult over you with praise, either because you are praiseworthy or because you sing with your praises.
Commentary on Zephaniah

Triflers (nugas), or, as Aquila translated, those carried away, who withdrew from you, I will gather, because they were of you; that is: Those who through vices and sins had fled from your bosom and had come under the power of demons will come to you when the state of all things has been restored, and you will by no means suffer reproaches any longer over your lost sons. What we have rendered nugas, let us know that in the Hebrew it is the Latin word itself, and for that reason it was set down by us just as it stood in the Hebrew, so that we may know that the Hebrew tongue is the mother of all tongues, a matter which it is not the time to discuss now. But I wonder that Aquila and the Seventy, where we translated they were, namely in the place where we said: I will gather, because they were of you: instead of they were chose to translate woe, or ὄι, which Aquila always uses not for lamenting but for calling and crying out. For Hai, of the verb whose beginning is sum, signifies the past tense in the plural number: they were, or they had been. I know that these things are tiresome to the reader; but if he notices that I am writing not controversies and declamations, nor exulting in commonplaces, but commentaries, and commentaries on the prophets, he will rather blame me if anywhere I have chosen to play in the manner of the rhetoricians than censure me for lingering, as is fitting, amid such great obscurities.
Commentary on Zephaniah

But since our hope is certain and the vows of the Jews are empty, let us now weave the present and last chapter according to the former understanding, and bring forward a testimony from Jesus son of Sirach: He who throws a stone on high throws it upon his own head. For since Zion and Jerusalem are set on high, whoever disparages Zion and Jerusalem and throws at her the stones of insults hurls them upon his own head, and his reproach will return upon his own head: And his pain and his iniquity will come down upon his crown. How many today reproach the soul that pursues the mysteries of God and wishes to see his peace, and say: He is mad, and drunk, and full of new wine; he flees the gatherings of men; he spurns delights, counts gold as mud, loves poverty alone. But those who are unbelievers reproach him even with the cross of Christ, and if ever they see him in distress and in temptation, they say: Where are your mercies, and the works of justice which you have performed? Why should I speak of unbelievers, when some leaders of the churches reproach men of this kind, and judge their life to be madness, and do not praise their present way of life but reproach them with their old sins? Nor do they hear that it is commanded: Do not upbraid a man who turns from his sins.
Commentary on Zephaniah

Behold, I will kill all who have afflicted you at that time, and I will save the lame one, and her who had been cast out I will gather; and I will set them for praise and for a name in all the land of their confusion. At that time when I will bring you in, and at the time when I will gather you; for I will give you for a name and for praise to all the peoples of the earth, when I have turned back your captivity before your eyes, says the Lord. LXX: Behold, I will act in you, for your sake, at that time, and I will save the pressed one, and the rejected one I will receive, and I will set them in glory; and named in all the earth. And they will be confounded at that time when I have done well to you; and at the time when I have received you, for I will give you named and in glory among all the peoples of the earth, when I have turned back your captivity before you, says the Lord. And this the synagogue, which does not limp but is maimed in both feet, promises itself at the coming of its Christ, whom it hopes is yet to come; and it thinks that all the nations which afflicted Israel are to be killed by the Lord, and the synagogue saved, and she who had received a bill of divorce gathered, and that they are to be set for praise and for a name in all the land of their captivity, in which they had formerly been confounded; and that this happens at the time when the captivity has been brought back to Jerusalem, and the temple built, and the remaining order of ceremonies observed. These things it promises itself, and therefore it does not repent, and while it hopes for uncertain things, it loses certain salvation. Nor do I wonder that the synagogue says these things, which, because it does not receive Christ, suffers in its eyes, and is bleary-eyed with Leah, and is not loved by Jacob, and, with Rachel taking her place, is neglected. I wonder at Christians, or rather half-Jews, who seem to themselves to be of the Church, speaking thus and professing those things which, if they are true, we believe in Christ in vain, and our whole mystery is taken away, and we are more wretched than all men, believing that he has come who has not come.
Commentary on Zephaniah

Woe therefore to him who has taken up and undertaken reproach, and has bound himself over to such a task as to disparage Zion and the city of God, for the Lord is the avenger of this injury to his city, and he will say to Zion: Behold, I will act in you for your sake, that is, I will carry out your vengeance, and I will save the afflicted one, or, as it is said in the Greek, the pressed one, so that the sense is: I will save her who at present, like the grape and the olive, has been so pressed and afflicted by temptations and pressures, as by the winepress and the beam, that she might make wine and oil, and that Jesus might drink of the wine in the kingdom of his Father, and be anointed with the oil above his fellows. I think that it was for the pressing out of such wine and oil that Job suffered many things, and that, after he had made the wine and the oil, he heard from the Lord: Do you think that I answered you otherwise than that you might appear just? As if he were speaking to the grape and the olive: Do you suppose that I pressed and afflicted and crushed you for any other reason than to press wine and oil out of you? There follows: And her who had been rejected I will receive. God seems to reject us when he leaves us to temptation. Hence Job too: The visitation, he says, of the Lord has looked upon me. And not only do the just speak and say: But now you have rejected and confounded us, as is written in Psalm 43 (44), but the Lord and Savior himself, in the person of the man whom he had assumed: But you, he says, have rejected and despised, you have put off your Christ; you have overturned the covenant of your servant. That it is the person of the just in Psalm 43 (44) who say: But now you have rejected and confounded us, is proved from what follows: All these things have come upon us, yet we have not forgotten you, nor have we acted wickedly in your covenant; nor has our heart turned back. Her, therefore, who seemed cast away in temptations the Lord will receive at the end, and will set them in glory and named in all the earth, namely the sons of the pressed and rejected one, that is, of the Church. But what other sons of the Church can we understand as named, except the apostles? Look, I pray you, at Peter and Paul and Matthew and John, and consider that what was promised to Abraham: I will magnify your name, has been accomplished in deed in them. Daily it is named in the Church, daily their name is magnified, not because it profits them to be named by us in the Church, but so that we, magnifying their name and reading over what they wrote, may obtain salvation.
Commentary on Zephaniah

At that time, he says, when the pressed and rejected one has been received, and her sons set in glory — for the Lord glories in his athletes when he sees them crowned, as he gloried over Job against the devil; hence the Apostle too, exulting in the progress of his disciples, says: Yes, by your glory — those who had been your adversaries and had brought reproach against you will be confounded; and then they will see that those whom they had thought wretched are happy, and that those whom they reckoned poor and cast down have become powerful and glorious; then they will see their captivity, through which in this age they had been subjugated under a harsh rule, brought back into the heavenly Jerusalem, and themselves rising again to reproach and to everlasting confusion. Grant to us, Jesus Christ, who are pressed and afflicted and rejected in this age, that you may receive us and set us in glory; let the water-snake (excetra) be confounded in time, let the hissings cease, let the venoms grow numb, and let its confusion profit for salvation. These things according to the Seventy. But since the Hebrew, except for the beginning, about which we spoke at the end of the preceding chapter, does not differ much from their translation, I do not think it needs exposition.

intro: THE PROPHECY OF SOPHONIAS. INTRODUCTION. Sophonias, whose name, saith St. Jerome, signifies "the watchman of the Lord," or "the hidden of the Lord," prophesied in the beginning of the reign of Josias. He was a native of Sarabatha, and of the tribe of Simeon, according to the more general opinion. He prophesied the punishments of the Jews, for their idolatry and other crimes; also the punishments that were to come on divers nations; the coming of Christ, the conversion of the Gentiles, the blindness of the Jews, and their conversion towards the end of the world. (Challoner) --- Some editions read, Ezechias. (Haydock) --- But this opinion is not well grounded no more than that of the Jews, who assert (Calmet) that all the ancestors mentioned by the prophets were endued with the prophetic spirit, for which reason Amos specifies none, as he was not the son of a prophet, Amos vii. 14. (St. Jerome) --- Sophonias appeared a little before Jeremias, Ezechiel, Baruch, and Daniel, foretelling the captivity and return of the two tribes, the destruction of various nations, the conversion of the Gentiles, and of the Jews also towards the end of the world. (Worthington) --- Many of the promises regard only the Christian Church. (Calmet)
